name: vc4asm
desc: Macro assembler for Broadcom VideoCore IV aka Raspberry Pi GPU
why: An assembler for the Raspberry Pi's VideoCore IV GPU, a door into a closed, rarely-touched processor.

brief.what_it_is: vc4asm is a macro assembler and disassembler for the Broadcom VideoCore IV GPU found in the Raspberry Pi. The assembler vc4asm takes QPU assembly source files (.qasm) and outputs a raw little-endian binary, an ARM ELF object file for ld or gcc, or C/C++ source and header files. The disassembler vc4dis takes hexadecimal or binary QPU machine code and writes assembler source. The current version on the homepage is 0.3.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says the QPU area is highly undocumented in the public domain, so the project aims to be a full-featured macro assembler and disassembler with constraint checking. It builds on earlier work by Pete Warden (qpu-asm), Eman, and Herman H Hermitage, and goes further by adding macros and functions.
brief.how_it_works: The author used the code of the hello_fft sample as a Rosetta Stone to learn the instruction encoding, and says the tool tries to stay downwardly compatible with the Broadcom tools. The assembler accepts several .qasm files, which are concatenated in order rather than linked as separate modules, and can include platform definitions such as vc4.qinc. The -V option checks VideoCore IV constraints, such as reading a register file address right after writing it. The disassembler's -M option suppresses emulated mov instructions so that a disassemble-then-reassemble round trip gives the same binary.

brief.install_notes: The source is on GitHub at github.com/maazl/vc4asm, and the homepage links to a Raspberry Pi 1 binary download. Building needs a C++11 compiler (the author says gcc 4.9 on current Raspbian works; Wheezy's gcc 4.7.2 fails on the disassembler, and gcc 4.8 can be installed on Wheezy) and CMake. The source should build on other platforms too. Running the test cases needs Perl. The sample programs only build and run on a Raspberry Pi model. They need the vc4 display driver to be off, since the GPU cannot be used while that driver runs. The author recommends installing the vcio2 driver so the samples do not need root, but vcio2 blocks direct hardware access, which makes small hello_fft transforms significantly slower.
brief.standout: It supports macros and functions, which the author says are poorly documented elsewhere. It also has constraint checking (-V) and a disassembler that can round-trip code. Its hello_fft shader was hand-optimized for this assembler, with about 40% less code and roughly 9% less run time than GPU_FFT 3.0, and the author says it will not build with another assembler.
brief.status: Unknown. The homepage gives version 0.3 and says to see the change log for details, but I saw no release date. The GitHub README shows no last-commit date, and the changelog link was not fetched. The homepage's Known problems section says there are too few test cases, so bugs are likely.
brief.caveats: The samples run only on Raspberry Pi hardware and need root or the vcio2 driver, and the vc4 display driver must be off. The author says there are insufficient test cases, so bugs are likely. The assembler is aimed at QPU code for a GPU that the author calls rarely documented. The hello_fft shader only builds with this assembler. In the benchmark table, the 214-point FFT is slower with the optimized code, and the author does not know why. Some timings are marked unstable. The build needs C++11 and CMake, and the scripts are .Cmd files. The page does not state a license. The homepage was reachable.

judge.reason: A macro assembler, disassembler, and constraint checker for an obscure, poorly documented Raspberry Pi GPU opens a compelling door into its instruction set.

entry.title: vc4asm
entry.tldr: An assembler and disassembler for the Raspberry Pi's VideoCore IV GPU, a barely documented processor you can write machine code for yourself.
entry.deeper_look:
vc4asm is a macro assembler for the QPU cores inside the Broadcom VideoCore IV, the GPU in the original Raspberry Pi. It reads `.qasm` source and writes a raw little-endian binary, an ARM ELF object for `ld` or `gcc`, or C/C++ source and header files. Its companion `vc4dis` goes the other way, turning hex or binary QPU machine code back into assembler source.

The author built it because, in their words, "this area is highly undocumented in the public domain." With little documentation to go on, the instruction encoding was worked out using the `hello_fft` sample as a Rosetta Stone. The project builds on earlier assemblers by Pete Warden (qpu-asm), Eman, and Herman H Hermitage, and adds macros, functions, and constraint checking.

The constraint checker (`-V`) catches hardware rules that are easy to break by hand, such as reading a register file address right after writing it. The disassembler's `-M` option suppresses emulated `mov` instructions, so disassembling and reassembling gives back the same binary. That round trip makes it a decent tool for taking apart existing GPU code.

The idea underneath is that the GPU is just another small processor with its own instruction set, and with an assembler you can program it directly instead of going through a graphics API. The homepage includes a hand-optimized FFT shader as proof, with about 40% less code and roughly 9% less run time than GPU_FFT 3.0.
entry.install:
brew install vc4asm
# Assembling and disassembling work anywhere. Running the sample GPU programs needs a Raspberry Pi with the vc4 display driver turned off.

Assembles the homepage's FFT example into a raw binary, pulling in the platform definitions from vc4.qinc.
Prints the disassembler's options, including `-M` for reassemblable output and `-b` for a base address.

entry.whats_unique: It gives you macros, functions, and constraint checking for a GPU that almost nobody documents, plus a disassembler that can round-trip. Its optimized FFT shader builds only with this assembler.
entry.caveats: The author says there are too few test cases so bugs are likely, the release date is unclear, and the samples run only on Raspberry Pi hardware with the vc4 display driver off.
